title: Why You Should Never Allow Students To Make Up Work
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues firmly against the now-common practice of allowing students to retake tests, turn in late work without penalty, or ignore deadlines. His central claim is that leniency around deadlines guarantees students fall further behind, since new material depends on mastery of what came before, and that flexible deadlines actively invite cheating as students wait until the last possible moment. He extends the argument psychologically, claiming that endless second chances teach laziness, entitlement, and excuse-making rather than the discipline and responsibility students need for adult life, and can even contribute to a sense of meaninglessness and depression when goals carry no real stakes. The concrete stance is a hard line: no retakes, no makeups, no negotiated extensions, framed not as harshness but as a form of care and leadership rare in today's educational climate. He acknowledges students may not appreciate the firmness until years later, but insists it is precisely what prepares them for real-world accountability.
points: Retakes and makeup work guarantee students fall behind because new lessons build on unmastered prior material.
Flexible deadlines are said to invite cheating, since students wait until the last moment when the only option left is to copy or cut corners.
Endless second chances are framed as teaching laziness and entitlement rather than responsibility.
Firm deadlines are reframed as an act of genuine care and leadership, even though students may not appreciate it until years later.
quotes: But allowing students to retake tests, make up assignments, and ignore deadlines is something you should never do.
Your students can’t stay up to date with your current lessons when they haven’t mastered the previous and prerequisite material.
By giving chance after chance, you’re very effectively teaching students to be lazy, undisciplined, and unemployable. Discipline is learned through hard deadlines.
Without goals, objectives, and due dates with real stakes, life very quickly loses meaning.
Without standards to meet, students become entitled. They begin to believe that everything can be put off, ignored, or negotiated to their liking.
Although a gift your students may not understand or appreciate until years later, holding them to a standard required for success in school and beyond is nonetheless precious.
